opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the original SWE-bench is a really clever idea. You take real GitHub issues from popular Python repos, along with the pull requests that actually fixed them, and you use the tests that came with those PRs to check whether a model's patch solves the problem. That's great because it's grounded in real-world software engineering instead of toy puzzles.

The problem is that because it was assembled automatically, a fair number of the tasks are, frankly, not solvable as written. Sometimes the issue description is really underspecified. It says something like "this behaves weirdly" without saying what the correct behavior should be. And then the hidden tests are checking for one very specific implementation. Other times the tests check for something the issue never mentions at all, like a particular function name or a specific error message string that you'd only know if you'd seen the original PR. And there were some cases where the environment setup was just flaky, so even a correct solution could fail.

So when you look at a model scoring, say, 30 or 40 percent, you don't really know how much of the remaining 60 percent is the model failing versus the benchmark asking for something impossible. That puts a ceiling on the benchmark and adds a lot of noise, and once models get good, that noise starts to dominate.

What OpenAI did with Verified was bring in professional software engineers to manually review the tasks and filter out the ones that are underspecified, have unfair tests, or have broken setups. You end up with a subset of 500 problems where you can be pretty confident that a good engineer, given just the issue and the codebase, could actually solve it and pass the tests. That makes the scores a lot more meaningful. When a model fails there, it's much more likely to be a real failure of the model rather than an artifact of the dataset.

For us building agents, that was really valuable, because it meant improvements on the benchmark actually tracked improvements in real capability, instead of us chasing noise.

r001.rationale: It says some hidden tests require a specific error-message string the issue never mentions and that would only be known from the original PR.

r002.rationale: It describes professional engineers manually reviewing tasks and filtering out underspecified or unfair ones, leaving tasks an engineer could solve from the issue and codebase.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the original SWE-bench was a really great idea: take real GitHub issues from real Python repos, give the model the issue text and the repo, and see if it can produce a patch that makes the hidden tests pass. That's a huge step up from toy coding problems. But when we actually sat down and looked at the individual tasks, a lot of them were kind of broken in ways that had nothing to do with whether the model was a good software engineer.

There were basically three big categories. The first was underspecified issues. The issue would say something like "this function behaves weirdly in this case," and then the hidden test would check for a very specific error message or a very specific return type that was never mentioned anywhere. So a model could fix the bug in a completely reasonable way and still fail, because it didn't guess the exact string the maintainer happened to write. That's not testing coding ability, that's testing mind reading.

The second category was tests that were just too strict or too narrow. The test might check implementation details, or it would only pass if you made the change in exactly the way the original PR did, even though there were other totally valid approaches.

And then the third was tasks where the environment was flaky, or the test setup was broken, or the task required something that wasn't really possible from the information given, so even a perfect engineer couldn't solve it.

So what we did with OpenAI and the SWE-bench team was go through a sample and have human annotators, who were actual software engineers, rate each task on things like: is the issue well specified enough that you could solve it, and are the tests fair given that specification. And then we filtered down to the roughly five hundred tasks that passed, which became SWE-bench Verified.

The reason this matters is that if a benchmark has a bunch of unsolvable tasks baked in, it caps the score and it adds a bunch of noise. You end up measuring how well a model happens to match the quirks of the dataset rather than how good it is at fixing bugs. With Verified, when a model fails, we're much more confident it actually failed, and when it improves, we're more confident it's a real improvement in capability.

r001.rationale: It says hidden tests could require a specific error message that was never mentioned, so the model could not infer the expected string from the task information.

r002.rationale: It describes human annotators reviewing whether tasks were sufficiently specified and filtering out those that could not be solved from the available information.

astra-6.text:
The core issue is that failing a SWE-bench task doesn’t always mean the model failed to solve the engineering problem. Sometimes the issue description doesn’t give you enough information to know what’s expected, or the tests require a very specific implementation even though another solution would be valid. So you’re mixing up model failures with problems in the benchmark itself.

SWE-bench Verified tries to address that by having humans review the tasks and select a subset where the problem is sufficiently well specified and the tests are a fair way to evaluate the solution. That makes the score a cleaner signal of whether the model can actually fix the issue.

r001.rationale: The response mentions underspecified issues and tests requiring a specific implementation, but does not say that a test may require an exact error-message string that cannot be inferred from the task information.

r002.rationale: It says humans review tasks and select a subset where the problem is sufficiently well specified, which conveys excluding tasks that cannot be solved from the supplied information.

sol-6.1.text:
The core issue is that a failure on SWE-bench doesn’t necessarily mean the model failed to solve the problem. Sometimes the issue description doesn’t contain enough information to know what the expected fix is. And sometimes the tests are too specific to the original developer’s implementation, so a different, valid solution would still fail.

SWE-bench Verified tries to clean that up by having humans review the tasks and select a subset where the issue is well specified and the tests are a fair check of whether you solved it. That makes the score a more useful measure of the model’s ability to do software engineering, with less noise from problems in the benchmark itself.

r002.rationale: It says humans review tasks and select a subset with well-specified issues, which communicates excluding tasks that cannot be solved from the supplied information.
